paragraphs: If you are willing to clarify what problem the business actually needs to solve before deciding how to build the system, this occupation is worth exploring further; skipping requirements and going straight to a solution or product choice can create a large gap between expectations and reality.

If you can accept that a solution must satisfy business, technical, data and compliance constraints together, and are willing to document tradeoffs, this work will use that ability every day; expecting to produce only the technically optimal solution will lead to disappointment.

If you are willing to repeatedly align interfaces, fields and workflows with users, developers, operations staff and suppliers, and accept validation and training both before and after delivery, this work suits you; wanting only to complete tasks alone will make adjustment difficult.

If you are willing to update documents and reassess the scope of impact when requirements change, rather than proceed on verbal agreements, this occupation is worth exploring further; undocumented changes can directly become deployment incidents.

If you are willing to keep tracking changes in technology stacks, data tools and compliance requirements and turn them into actionable solution adjustments, you can sustain this work over the long term; stopping updates will quickly make solutions obsolete.
Before starting, confirm that you can organize vague business requests into verifiable fields, workflows and acceptance criteria, and document them.

Trial method: write a one-page requirements brief for a fictional business scenario, such as redesigning an expense reimbursement workflow, including the current workflow, proposed changes, fields and rules, acceptance criteria and two risks.

Boundary: the exercises and judgments on this page are only for self-checking. They do not constitute hiring criteria, qualification recognition or authorization to operate or deploy real systems; work involving real systems and data must follow your organization's rules.

Note: if your goal is to write code, develop security policies or design network architecture over the long term, this occupation is a useful adjacent direction but a different role; those directions require additional coding, security or architecture abilities and corresponding qualifications.

One-sentence summary: this work centers on translating business problems into system solutions that can be implemented, verified and maintained, and suits people willing to clarify requirements, coordinate stakeholders and take responsibility for delivery results.

The official occupation analyzes data-processing problems in science, engineering, business and other areas, and develops or implements complex applications, systems management or network solutions. The editorial grouping has three work areas: requirements/solutions; integration/testing; support/improvement. Work may involve programming, code correction and cost-benefit analysis; verify actual responsibilities and authority with the organization.
Requirements briefs and system design documents
Interviews and observation → organize workflows and data → define system objectives → design inputs and outputs → assess candidate solutions → confirm with management
Integration implementation records and testing and acceptance results

Check software and hardware requirements → coordinate installation and configuration → connect interfaces and data → perform testing and monitoring → address defects and regression testing → record tests and changes
Fix faults and program problems → train users and write instructions → monitor operating metrics → improve the system based on feedback

This page compares computer systems analysts with adjacent occupations across six dimensions: core purpose, main objects and evidence, core process, main outputs, accountable parties, and entry requirements and licensing. Tasks and tools may overlap, but system design authority, architecture decisions, operations and maintenance responsibilities, and resource allocation authority do not transfer merely because tasks are similar.

Core purposes of adjacent occupations: computer and information systems managers coordinate departmental resources and delivery; computer systems engineers and architects design systems and architecture; network and computer systems administrators ensure operation; computer network architects design network solutions.
Analyze business and technical problems and design, integrate and improve systems so existing systems better support business objectives.

Objects and evidence for adjacent occupations: departmental resources and budgets (managers), system and architecture specifications (systems engineers and architects), and network and server operation (administrators and network architects).

Business workflows and data, existing systems and interfaces, users and job tasks; evidence consists of interview and observation records, workflow and data documents, system logs and requirements confirmation.
Management, architecture, operations and analysis tasks may overlap; verify workflows with the actual organization rather than impose a fixed sequence for all roles based on titles.
Interviews and observation → organize workflows and data → define objectives and specifications → design and integrate → test and deploy → train and improve.

Requirements briefs, system design and interface documents, testing and change records, user instructions and training materials, and deployment and rollback records.
Accountable parties in adjacent occupations: managers are responsible for resources and delivery; systems engineers and architects for system design; administrators for operational availability.

Analysts and project leads are responsible for the completeness of requirements confirmation, design evidence, and testing and change records. Data permissions and deployment approvals must follow the organization's rules; this page does not replace employer policies or legal advice.

Check one: are business objectives and the current situation clearly documented?

Document current workflows, participating roles, data sources and pain points before discussing changes; designing without confirming the current situation often moves existing problems into the system.
Check two: are definitions and data consistent?
The same field can mean different things in different departments; align definitions, sources and update frequency before deciding how the system should process and display it.
Check three: are specifications and acceptance criteria verifiable?
Replace “the system should be easy to use” with verifiable conditions, such as who can do what, how long it takes and how exceptions are reported, and include them in the requirements brief.
Check four: are interfaces with existing systems feasible?
Confirm interface methods, data flows, permissions and failure handling, and assess impacts on current operation; confirm with systems administrators and suppliers when necessary.
Check five: are change and testing records complete?
Requirements changes should document reasons, scope of impact and versions; testing should record cases, results and environments so colleagues can reproduce them.
Check six: is someone responsible for deployment and rollback?
Before deployment, specify rollback conditions and responsible parties and prepare data backups and switchover steps; after deployment, validate key business workflows as planned.

entries: Requirements | Interview people and map business workflows | Interview clients and users and observe work tasks; identify who handles which data at each stage to produce a current-state description and list of problems.

Design | Define system objectives and specifications | Define system scope, inputs and outputs, processing rules and acceptance criteria from the current situation and business objectives, and assess candidate solutions' compatibility with existing systems.

Integration | Coordinate installation and interface configuration | Coordinate software and hardware installation and configure interfaces and data flows according to the design so systems within the organization can exchange information.

Testing | Perform tests and monitor operation | Write test cases covering normal and exceptional paths and record environments and results; after deployment, monitor performance and error logs to locate and correct problems.

Improvement | Improve system workflows using operating data | Propose improvements based on operating metrics and user feedback, assess the scope of impact and schedule changes, adjusting workflows and training materials when necessary.
Collaboration | Train users and maintain documentation | Write user instructions and train users; maintain design, testing and change documents so others can take over.

The table below compares computer systems analysts with five adjacent occupations using the same dimensions: each direction first describes core work and outputs, then key differences from this occupation, and finally when choosing that direction may be more suitable.

Engineers and architects are responsible for overall system architecture and integration design; this occupation focuses on turning business requirements into specifications and implementation plans and usually does not bear final responsibility for architecture decisions.
If you prefer architecture decisions and technology selection, explore engineers and architects; if you prefer clarifying business requirements and implementing solutions, explore this occupation.
Design and integrate computer systems and overall architecture, producing system architecture, integration plans and technology selection recommendations.
Computer Systems Engineers and Architects

Administrators are responsible for system availability and daily maintenance; this occupation is responsible for requirements, design and deployment results and usually does not provide ongoing operational coverage.
If you prefer responsibility for continuous system operation and incident response, explore administrators; if you prefer requirements and solution design, explore this occupation.
Install, configure and maintain networks, servers and operating systems, producing available systems and operational monitoring and incident resolution records.
Network and Computer Systems Administrators

Managers are responsible for resources and delivery; this occupation is responsible for the basis of solutions and deployment results and does not hold departmental budget or personnel decision-making authority.

If you prefer coordinating resources and teams and taking responsibility for delivery results and budgets, explore management; if you prefer working closely with specific requirements and solutions, explore this occupation.
Coordinate IT department personnel, budgets, projects and service levels, producing departmental plans, budgets and delivery results.
Computer and Information Systems Managers
Network architects decide how networks are designed and expanded; this occupation uses network capabilities when designing solutions but is not responsible for network architecture decisions.
If you prefer network design and capacity planning, explore network architecture; if you prefer translating business needs into systems, explore this occupation.
Design and implement LAN, WAN and cloud network solutions, producing network designs and capacity and implementation documentation.
Computer Network Architects
Programmers are responsible for code correctness and maintainability; this occupation is responsible for requirements, design and integration, with coding only one means of implementation.
If you prefer writing code and debugging over the long term, explore programming; if you prefer defining requirements and design, explore this occupation.
Write, modify and test code and scripts, producing working programs and development documentation.
Computer Programmers
Security analysts are responsible for controls and incident response; this occupation must satisfy security requirements when designing solutions but does not define security policies.
If you prefer studying attack surfaces and developing security controls, explore security; if you prefer system solutions and deployment coordination, explore this occupation.
Plan, implement and monitor security measures, producing security policies, controls and incident reports.
Information Security Analysts

If you are deciding between two directions, first try a small experiment using a fictional business scenario: write a one-page requirements brief and acceptance criteria, then see whether you prefer refining requirements and solutions or working on architecture, operations and maintenance, or coding.

items.title: What Evidence Employers Usually Look For

values: Fictional Business Materials (Exercise Input)
Fictional scenario: a company's finance department wants to replace paper expense reimbursements with online approval; you are the analyst responsible for clarifying requirements.

Provided materials: current workflow (employee completes a paper form → supervisor signs → finance enters data → cashier pays, averaging 5 working days); fields (applicant, department, amount, expense type, invoice number, approver); current rules (amounts of 5000 yuan or more require second-level approval; travel expenses require an itinerary).

Missing materials: whether to integrate with the existing ERP, whether invoices need authenticity verification, and whether multiple legal entities are involved. State assumptions explicitly if your exercise requires these conditions.
Task Requirements
Write a one-page requirements brief including current and target workflows, fields and rules, acceptance criteria including exception paths, and two major risks and responses.
The requirements brief should specify which conditions business stakeholders confirm and which require joint assessment with development or operations.
Reference Deliverable (Can Be Derived From the Prompt)

The requirements brief should include: objectives (shorten approval cycles and retain records), workflow changes (online submission and approval, automatic finance aggregation), fields and rules (amount thresholds, expense types and attachment requirements), acceptance criteria (approval can finish within 2 working days, amounts and invoice information can be exported for checking), exception paths (missing approver, excessive amount, missing attachments), risks (data consistency in ERP integration and invoice authenticity requirements) and responses (start with a small pilot and clarify definitions and accountable parties).
The reference deliverable lists required elements only; its wording need not match the example, provided you can explain the basis for your judgments.
Boundaries and Conclusions That Cannot Be Inferred
This exercise tests only requirements mapping and documentation abilities; it does not evaluate real project results or constitute hiring or qualification judgments.
Work Sample One: Requirements Brief Collection

Deliverables: requirements briefs for two fictional scenarios, such as online expense reimbursement and automated inventory reconciliation, each including current workflows, fields and rules, acceptance criteria and exception paths.
Each brief should specify which definitions require confirmation by business stakeholders and which require assessment with developers.
Work Sample Two: System and Interface Design Description
Deliverable: an interface or data-flow design description including data sources, field mappings, failure handling and impact assessment for existing systems.
Include one rejected solution and the reason for rejecting it.
Work Sample Three: Testing and Deployment Checklist
Deliverables: a test-case list including normal and exception paths and a deployment and rollback steps checklist.
Tool Description

Deliverable: a one-page description listing the tools you use for data retrieval, workflow diagrams and documentation, and their purposes; do not include real company data, accounts or client information.

values: Day 1: Read a Requirements Document
Find a public requirements or product description document, mark the current situation, fields, rules and acceptance criteria, and note three points you want to confirm.
Day 2: Write the Current Workflow
For the fictional scenario of moving travel reimbursements online, draw or write the current workflow, including roles, fields and approval rules.
Day 3: Write Acceptance Criteria
Write 5 verifiable acceptance criteria for that scenario, including at least two exception paths.
Day 4: Define Fields and Their Meanings
List 8 core fields with meanings, sources, units and update frequencies, and mark two that may be ambiguous.
Day 5: Write Interface and Failure Handling Details
For one external dependency, such as an invoice authenticity verification service, write an interface description: data flows, failure scenarios and compensation methods.
Day 6: Write Testing and Deployment Checklists
List 6 test cases, including boundary values, and deployment steps and rollback conditions.
Day 7: Decide Whether to Continue
Return to this page's judgment checklist and write three reasons to continue and two conditions requiring caution.

entries: Specific change: can you break one business request into workflows, fields and acceptance criteria rather than merely describe the problem?
Facts and choices: do you prefer requirements and business analysis, system design and integration, or data and reporting?
Exercise demands: which step—documentation, aligning definitions or organizing reviews—drains you most, and can you accept its recurrence in projects?
Material boundaries: exercise materials are fictional or based on public sources; do not use real company data, accounts or client information.
Response to feedback: when someone points out unclear definitions in your requirements brief, are you willing to confirm them and align versions?
Interest in the process: are you willing to make workflows and data verifiable for acceptance even in projects without new technical toys?

Next step: if you are willing to continue through all six preceding steps, complete a full requirements and design cycle with a real de-identified business scenario and ask peers to review it; if one step is particularly draining, narrow your direction before further validation.
